item.title: These 4 built-in Windows recovery tools keep saving me from a clean install every time something breaks
item.itunes:title: These 4 built-in Windows recovery tools keep saving me from a clean install every time something breaks
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Given how many times Windows 11 throws seemingly messy and complex problems to solve, I'm willing to bet that almost every long-time user has been at the brink of wiping the OS and reinstalling it from scratch.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Not every user's workflow allows for the time to go down a long and arduous troubleshooting process, jumping from one Reddit thread or Microsoft Learn forum to another, and not every user can be expected to have the level of patience that these issues sometimes demand out of the blue.

But reinstalling an entire operating system comes with its own set of configuration headaches. You have to configure all your app and driver settings back again by hand, and doing so can often cost you more time than using Windows' own built-in recovery tools. The only thing you have to know is that they exist, and how to find them. Here are some native utilities that can save you hours before you clock out of work to fix a broken OS.

Fix problems using Windows Update

A reinstall that will leave all your files exactly where they were

I'll admit the sheer irony of opening the list with something that reinstalls your OS, but the path that I'm recommending makes sure that your files, programs, and drivers stay exactly the way as you configured them. To do this, you have to go into Settings > System > Recovery, where you'll find the option to "Fix problems using Windows Update". Besides that, you'll find an option to "reinstall now".

Let's say you found yourself in the unfortunate situation wherein Windows boots, but your system files and components are damaged, and your updates keep failing for one reason or another. This option lets you reinstall the current OS version while keeping your apps, files, and settings. What it does is that it downloads a repair copy of the last successfully installed update, which saves you the hassle of hunting down an ISO or reaching for a USB to flash.

My Windows install is ten years old, and a handful of maintenance habits are why it still runs like new

Essential maintenance keeps my old Windows 11 system running smoothly.

21
By  Brian Burgess

Uninstall Updates

It comes in handy whenever Patch Tuesday comes around

Some of the messes on Windows 11 come with an obvious culprit, and the latest update is usually the first suspect when things don't look right on my PC. If you've ever used your Windows PC for gaming and found glitches, artefacting, or anomalous behavior suddenly after you clicked "Update and shut down" the night before, you've probably already been in that position. I know that I did when Forza Horizon 5 worked fine the night before and the following day had broken shadows and textures.

Unfortunately, Microsoft has kept expanding the list of things that broke one thing or the other on Windows 11 this year, and there's no telling if it's a trend that'll cease anytime soon. Take the KB5074109 security update in January, for example, which left some devices running 24H2 and 25H2 unable to boot, and the only workaround was removing it from the recovery environment.

If you can still boot into your OS, you can head into Settings > Windows Update > Update history and choose to "Uninstall updates", pick the offender from the list, and remove it. If your OS flat out doesn't boot, it's possible to do it through the recovery environment under Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Uninstall updates.

Windows 11 will soon let you recover your PC from the cloud, and yes, it includes the drivers

Here's hoping it arrives in due time.

1
By  Simon Batt

Point-in-time restore

It's an undo button for your PC, with a 72-hour memory

If I've uninstalled the latest update and an issue on my PC still lingers, the next suspect is, well, me, or something that I did unwittingly. Luckily, Point-in-time restore offers a path out of whatever self-inflicted mess you've landed yourself in, and if you tinker a lot with your PC like I do, it's worth keeping this one in mind.

This feature reached general availability in June 2026, and from then on, Windows has been snapshotting the entire system drive roughly every 24 hours and retaining it for up to 72 hours. It's enabled by default on unmanaged PCs which have a Windows volume of 200GB or more.

Unlike all the other options that I've listed so far, this recovery method does touch your files, and that's a critical part of how it's designed. Otherwise, it couldn't undo the issues that you've accidentally caused. A restore will rewind everything on the drive, including all apps, files, and settings, so anything created after the snapshot is gone. Anything backed up to the cloud like OneDrive won't be affected, though. You can access it through the recovery environment via the troubleshooting menu.

This one Windows 11 update made my PC faster and consume less RAM, and I didn't change a single setting

There's no reason not to upgrade to 26H2

By  Abhinav Raj

Quick machine recovery

For the times when the problem isn't only on your PC

There are times when issues on your PC haven't been caused by you, and you can't fix them on your own. Such issues can occur for a wide variety of reasons, like a bad update or a driver knocking out a number of PCs, and on such occasions, the fix has to come from Microsoft.

For such occasions, it's worth knowing what Quick machine recovery is, and how you can find it. You probably already know that after several failed boots, Windows will automatically drop you into the recovery environment. What it does next is connect to the internet over Ethernet or Wi-Fi and check Windows Update for a fix from Microsoft. If there is one, it installs and the PC restarts.

This is on by default for Windows 11 Home and Pro PCs that aren't managed by an organization, and you can find the option to enable it under Settings > System > Recovery > Quick machine recovery. If you'd rather not wait for it to kick in, you can run it yourself through the recovery environment via Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Quick machine recovery.

These four tools can save you from hours of troubleshooting

The only thing that's almost certain about Microsoft's OS is that it will continue to break in new ways, and that's exactly why the tools I've mentioned should be a part of everyone's troubleshooting arsenal. More often than not, they'll save you from jumping from one troubleshooting thread to another or reinstalling the OS right from the beginning, both of which are hassles anyone with a busy workflow wants to avoid.

item.title: Your spare PCIe slot may not actually be free, and checking your manual matters
item.itunes:title: Your spare PCIe slot may not actually be free, and checking your manual matters
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Using the second or third PCIe slot on your motherboard is usually pretty straightforward. Whether you're installing a capture card, a network adapter, or even an expansion card to add more NVMe SSDs, you'd naturally assume that you can just plug it in and call it a day. After all, when you see three full-length slots on your motherboard, there's really no reason to think otherwise. Except things aren't always that simple, especially on modern motherboards where PCIe and M.2 slots can share lanes and limit the bandwidth available to your GPU.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I ran into this limitation with my MSI MPG X870E Carbon Wi-Fi motherboard, which I bought when I upgraded to AM5 earlier this year. But even my old Asus ROG Strix X570-E had similar restrictions, so this isn't exactly a new problem. The difference now is that more high-speed M.2 slots compete for PCIe lanes, making it easier to hit these limits without realizing it. That's why it's important to dig through your motherboard's manual and understand how its PCIe lanes are distributed before you buy an expansion card.

Your PC's unused PCIe slot beats M.2 for expansion — and it's not even close

PCIe slots offer greater bandwidth, power delivery, and versatility

8
By  Tanveer Singh

That PCIe slot could share lanes with your GPU

Populating it can cut your GPU's available bandwidth in half

Both my motherboards are perfect examples of why you shouldn't blindly populate your PCIe and M.2 slots. Sure, you can install an expansion card if you want, but depending on which slot you use, there can be compromises. On my MSI MPG X870E Carbon Wi-Fi, the primary PCIe slot, which houses my GPU, shares its 16 PCIe lanes from the CPU with the second PCIe slot and the M2_2 connector. This means if I install an expansion card in the second slot or install an NVMe in M.2_2, the motherboard needs to split those lanes into an x8/x4/x4 configuration.

The result is my RTX 4090 running at PCIe 4.0 x8 instead of x16, effectively cutting its available PCIe bandwidth in half. However, this isn't an issue if I populate the third PCIe slot on my board because that's connected to the chipset rather than sharing the CPU lanes allocated to my GPU. Even my ROG Strix X570-E board dropped the primary slot to x8 if I populated the second PCIe slot. Either way, your GPU running at x8 instead of x16 doesn't mean your gaming performance would drop by half since most games don't come close to saturating a PCIe 4.0 x16 connection in the first place.

Just because it's a full-length slot doesn't mean it's x16

Some PCIe slots are only wired for x4 or x8

The second PCIe slot on your motherboard may look identical to the primary slot that you use for your GPU, but that doesn't necessarily mean it provides the same bandwidth. For instance, the second slot on my X870E Carbon Wi-Fi tops out at PCIe 5.0 x4, while the third runs at PCIe 4.0 x4 through the chipset. So even though those secondary slots are physically long enough to fit a GPU, they may only have four or eight lanes each, depending on the motherboard.

Of course, this is a non-issue if all you're planning to install is something like a capture card or a network adapter, since they typically don't need more than an x4 connection anyway. However, if you want to install a high-end PCIe expansion card like the Asus Hyper M.2 x16 for adding four NVMe drives, an x4 slot simply won't cut it. Even if the card physically fits, you may not even be able to use all four SSDs, since that depends on how many lanes the slot provides and whether your motherboard supports PCIe bifurcation.

Losing half your PCIe lanes isn't a big deal, though

But that doesn't mean you should ignore the trade-offs

Like I said earlier, running your GPU at x8 instead of x16 isn't going to tank your frame rates. For instance, if you have an RTX 5090 in a motherboard that supports PCIe 5.0, dropping to x8 means it still gets the same bandwidth as PCIe 4.0 x16, which is plenty. I'm not saying there's no performance difference, but if the gap between PCIe 5.0 x16 and PCIe 3.0 x16 is only around 1-4% in Gamers Nexus' testing, it's hard to argue that dropping to PCIe 5.0 x8 or even PCIe 4.0 x8 is a dealbreaker.

Now, if you're using an older motherboard with PCIe 3.0 slots, that's a different story. Dropping your GPU from PCIe 3.0 x16 to x8 could actually have a noticeable impact on gaming performance, especially in titles that need to transfer a lot of data between RAM and VRAM. And it's not just the GPU you need to worry about. Depending on the motherboard, populating the second PCIe slot can also reduce the bandwidth available to the M.2 slot that shares lanes with it, or even disable that slot altogether.

Check the manual and save yourself a headache

I'm not saying the second PCIe slot is pointless just because it shares lanes with your GPU or an M.2 slot. You can still use it for all sorts of expansion cards, but you need to know what you're getting yourself into. That's why it's worth spending a few minutes in the manual to see how the PCIe lanes are distributed and whether filling one slot comes at the expense of another. Next time you upgrade your motherboard, dig through the spec sheet and check the fine print in the PCIe specifications. The last thing you want is to spend money on an expansion card only to realize your motherboard can't fully support it.

The second PCIe slot on your motherboard may look identical to the primary slot that you use for your GPU, but that doesn't necessarily mean it provides the same bandwidth. So even though those secondary slots are physically long enough to fit a GPU, they may only have four or eight lanes each, depending on the motherboard.

Of course, this is a non-issue if all you're planning to install is something like a capture card or a network adapter, since they typically don't need more than an x4 connection anyway. Even if the card physically fits, you may not even be able to use all four SSDs, since that depends on how many lanes the slot provides and whether your motherboard supports PCIe bifurcation.

But that doesn't mean you should ignore the trade-offs

Like I said earlier, running your GPU at x8 instead of x16 isn't going to tank your frame rates. For instance, if you have an RTX 5090 in a motherboard that supports PCIe 5.0, dropping to x8 means it still gets the same bandwidth as PCIe 4.0 x16, which is plenty. I'm not saying there's no performance difference, but if the gap between PCIe 5.0 x16 and PCIe 3.0 x16 is only around 1-4% in Gamers Nexus' testing, it's hard to argue that dropping to PCIe 5.0 x8 or even PCIe 4.0 x8 is a dealbreaker.

Now, if you're using an older motherboard with PCIe 3.0 slots, that's a different story. Dropping your GPU from PCIe 3.0 x16 to x8 could actually have a noticeable impact on gaming performance, especially in titles that need to transfer a lot of data between RAM and VRAM. And it's not just the GPU you need to worry about. Depending on the motherboard, populating the second PCIe slot can also reduce the bandwidth available to the M.2 slot that shares lanes with it, or even disable that slot altogether.

Check the manual and save yourself a headache

I'm not saying the second PCIe slot is pointless just because it shares lanes with your GPU or an M.2 slot. You can still use it for all sorts of expansion cards, but you need to know what you're getting yourself into. That's why it's worth spending a few minutes in the manual to see how the PCIe lanes are distributed and whether filling one slot comes at the expense of another. Next time you upgrade your motherboard, dig through the spec sheet and check the fine print in the PCIe specifications. item.title: I used Spotify, YouTube Music, and Plexamp on Android Auto for a month, and the self-hosted one won
item.itunes:title: I used Spotify, YouTube Music, and Plexamp on Android Auto for a month, and the self-hosted one won
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I can’t drive without music playing, and Android Auto makes it easy to bring whichever music app you prefer into the car. I spent a month switching between Spotify, YouTube Music, and Plexamp, which plays music from my own Plex server.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Having access to an enormous streaming catalog is useful, but I also have a collection of music I’ve deliberately picked, and I want to get more out of it. Plexamp gives that collection proper discovery features, so you can start with a song you like and find your way back to albums you’ve neglected. After a month with all three, Plexamp is surprisingly the one I want to keep using in the car.

My own music gets proper discovery features

Rediscovering the collection I already love

Everything in my Plex library is there because I chose to add it. That already gives me a pretty good starting point when I want something to listen to during a drive, even if I just hit shuffle. Of course, you can curate playlists on Spotify and YouTube Music too, but with Plexamp, my entire collection is made up of music I actually like. I don't mind letting an algorithm decide what plays next once I've already decided which songs it can choose from.

But Plexamp goes beyond shuffling your music. Its Sonic Analysis features actually analyze the audio to find similarities between songs and albums in your library. You can start Track Radio from a song you like, and Plexamp will put together a queue of similar-sounding music from your own collection. There's also Album Radio, which takes a similar approach with entire albums, and Mixes for You, which creates mixes based on your listening history.

I keep choosing Plexamp over YouTube Music and Spotify because it forces me to approach music discovery differently. It lets me rediscover an album I haven't listened to in years or a song I've completely forgotten about. YouTube Music also lets you upload your own music, but those uploads don't influence its recommendations. Plexamp makes much better use of the music I already own.

I ripped my CDs again after 20 years of old MP3s, and it's the best audio upgrade I've made in ages

I got rid of crappy sounding MP3's and upgraded my audio to better quality FLAC rips.

17
By  Brian Burgess

The playback features make longer drives easier

Smoother transitions and fewer volume adjustments

When you’re playing music from different albums and decades, the volume can vary considerably between recordings. Reaching for the volume control every few songs gets annoying, especially in the car. Plexamp has a loudness-leveling feature that helps keep playback consistent across tracks. Spotify has normalization too, but I have learned to appreciate having that feature built into the player handling my own collection.

Plexamp also has an interesting feature called Sweet Fades. It uses loudness analysis to figure out where two tracks should overlap and adjusts the transition accordingly. Other music apps offer similar features, but I find it more interesting in Plexamp because it works with my own music library. It also supports gapless playback for continuous albums and live recordings, so you don't get awkward pauses between tracks that are supposed to flow into each other.

Plexamp also lets you configure pre-caching, which prepares upcoming music before you need it. That’s useful when your route takes you through patches of poor reception, although how much playback it can cover depends on what’s already cached.

I get more control over everyday listening

My playlists and devices follow my rules

I like having control over how often a song comes back into rotation. Just because a song is one of my favorites doesn't mean I want to hear it every time I go for a drive. Plex's smart playlists let you control this by combining rules like a minimum star rating and songs that haven't been played in the past seven days. As your listening history changes, the playlist updates automatically, so you don't have to add and remove songs manually.

Spotify has shuffle options that help mix things up, but I prefer having more control over what comes up next. For example, I can create a playlist of my favorite songs that I haven't listened to in the past month or give frequently played tracks a break for a week. Once you've set the rules, you can save the smart playlist and access it directly through Plexamp on Android Auto.

Another advantage I've found useful is playing music independently on multiple devices. Spotify and YouTube Music restrict simultaneous playback on the same account, so if someone starts playing music on a device at home, it can interrupt whatever you're listening to in the car. You can get around this with separate accounts on a family plan, but Plex lets you run independent streams from the same server, as long as your server has the resources and your settings allow it.

This means I can have one playlist running at home and listen to something completely different in the car without the two devices interfering with each other. Since I'm already hosting my own music collection, I like having that flexibility.

Plexamp has earned its place here

After a month with all three apps, I’m sticking with Plexamp for my drives. I already put effort into choosing and maintaining my music collection, and having a player that makes it this useful gives me a reason to keep building it.

item.title: I replaced three cloud subscriptions with my own server, and Tailscale makes it work anywhere
item.itunes:title: I replaced three cloud subscriptions with my own server, and Tailscale makes it work anywhere
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Saving money is one of the big reasons people can get into self-hosting, though whether that actually works out really depends on what you're doing with your server. Just replacing cloud storage with a home server may not actually be cheaper, but once you start replacing enough services, it can make a positive difference.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

For my part, my self-hosting server lets me sync my passwords, photos, and notes across all my devices, and I can access them from anywhere thanks to Tailscale. That has allowed me to replace three whole cloud plans I used to pay for, and I don't see myself going back.

Bitwarden syncs my passwords

Don't need the premium plan anymore

There are plenty of great password managers out there, including some solid free options like KeePassXC. But I've always heard good things about Bitwarden, so that's where I eventually landed, and initially, the premium plan seemed like a requirement, especially with it providing integration with one-time authentication codes. It wasn't overly expensive, but it's still a cost I didn't really want.

Thankfully, Bitwarden also offers the option to connect to a self-hosted server, and that comes at no cost. I simply had to create a Vaultwarden server, connect my Bitwarden apps and extensions to it, and I was ready to go. Bitwarden updates and saves my vault information locally, so I don't need a persistent connection all the time, but when I do, Tailscale allows me to connect to my server back home and get the latest information for signing in to my other services.

I moved every 2FA code out of Google and Microsoft Authenticator, and losing my phone isn't a disaster anymore

Bitwarden and Vaultwarden changed my life for the better

8
By  João Carrasqueira

I really love the integration with one-time authentication codes, because it addresses the worst part about using them. Bitwarden brings up the codes I need right as I need them, and it all works seamlessly. No need to hunt for my phone to access my authenticator app, it just works on any device I have.

My family photos are all on Immich

Goodbye, OneDrive (and Google Photos)

The biggest savings I got from self-hosting, however, was actually in the form of my photos, documents, and other files, which I used to store on OneDrive. This is a fairly expensive subscription that cost me $70 per year when I still had it, though the same plan now costs $100/year thanks to Copilot integration.

Self-hosting allowed me to move all my photos to Immich, a self-hosted gallery that has a modern UI very reminiscent of Google Photos. It looks and feels modern, it lets me organize pictures into albums, and it even supports locally-hosted facial recognition so I can find pictures of a specific person more quickly. Map data is also saved if I want it to be, I can go over potential duplicates and clean up my gallery, and there are new features being added all the time. It's great.

Immich is the first self-hosted Google Photos alternative my family actually uses

Immich combines a simple UI with robust image management and backup features, all while running on my local server

5
By  Ayush Pande

I'm only counting this as one subscription because it's my own, but Immich also stores my wife's photos, and she used to pay for Google One to store them, so we're technically saving on two subscriptions here.

Likewise, our documents are stored on Nextcloud, which offers an intuitive UI for managing files and can be expanded with all kinds of apps, including a built-in Office suite for editing documents.

Obsidian syncs for free, too

Who needs Obsidian sync?

Finally, there's the matter of notes, and one of the most popular was to keep notes these days is Obsidian. I used to use OneNote, but I'm trying to move away from Microsoft products, and it was frustrating to realize that to sync my notes on Obsidian, I'd have to pay $4 a month for Obsidian Sync.

Thankfully, Obsidian community plugins come to the rescue here, and LiveSync is a great one. I can deploy a new LiveSync server relatively easily and then connect my apps to it to keep all my notes in sync across devices. It's exactly the experience I expected after using OneNote for so long, though arguably it's even faster and more reliable.

I turned Obsidian into my personal operating system with just one vault

One vault to organize absolutely everything.

2
By  Parth Shah

Tailscale is free, but there's a catch

You may need more than that

Tailscale allows me to access all of these servers remotely and cut down on subscription costs, which is great. Tailscale itself is free and supports up to three users this way, so it's perfect for my wife and myself. However, I would be remiss not to mention that there's another cost you may have to deal with here: a domain.

You can probably get away with accessing some of these services remotely by just connecting to the IP addresses directly, but things like Bitwarden and Obsidian require an HTTPS connection with a verifiable security certificate, which usually means you need to use something like a reverse proxy to encrypt the connection, and that means buying a domain.

I built an always‑on VPN gateway with a Raspberry Pi Zero to access my home lab from anywhere

It's perfect when I want to work on my home lab projects from external networks

12
By  Ayush Pande

Still, the cost associated with my personal domain is just $12 for an entire year, and that's less than Bitwarden, which is the cheapest subscription of the bunch at around $20 per year. It's still easily worth it, and that's not even including the privacy and security benefits of having all my data stored on my own server.

I'm not going back to cloud services

Being able to stop spending this kind of money on cloud services is one of the big motivators that got me into self-hosting, and these three services make it clearer than any other. Add the privacy benefits and the fact that all this data is in my hands, and it makes self-hosting all the more worthwhile.

Bitwarden and Vaultwarden changed my life for the better

The biggest savings I got from self-hosting, however, was actually in the form of my photos, documents, and other files, which I used to store on OneDrive. It's perfect when I want to work on my home lab projects from external networks

Add the privacy benefits and the fact that all this data is in my hands, and it makes self-hosting all the more worthwhile.

item.itunes:summary:
Unless you've been living under a rock for the past year, you know about the PC hardware crisis we're going through. It started with RAM, but soon engulfed GPUs, SSDs, and even hard drives. Storage may not be a priority for gamers, but NAS and home lab users need tons of it at affordable prices. And that combination has all but disappeared if you look at consumer and NAS drives.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

If you've been looking to buy new hard drives, paying $350–$450 for an 8TB–12TB NAS drive has probably felt insane. Even 8TB consumer HDDs are going for around $300, so the situation is bad all around. In this market, the only way out is to look at pre-owned enterprise drives, specifically of the SAS variety. With a cheap adapter, you can use them with your DIY NAS, beating the market without losing out on performance.

4 reasons you should save money and repurpose old hard drives into a NAS

Using old drives inside your NAS can be a good idea whether you want to store some backups or save money.

2
By  Rich Edmonds

Overpriced storage has hit NAS users the most

The old rules no longer apply

  • Credit: Rawpixel
  • Credit: Rawpixel

The "RAMageddon" headlines focus mostly on RAM, SSDs, and GPUs, but NAS owners have been lamenting hard drive pricing ever since the hardware shortage hit our shores. The core hardware for building your own NAS doesn't need to be fancy; almost any old PC can be repurposed as a home NAS. The main concern is storage—buying the right kind and doing so without blowing your budget.

For years, NAS owners have used regular HDDs, NAS hard drives, and even SSDs for their storage needs, but the last 12 months have upended the natural order. Capacious drives are out of reach of the vast majority of DIY NAS owners and enthusiasts, delaying or shelving their plans. Even the pre-owned market for consumer and NAS HDDs has caught on, closing another door to potentially affordable storage.

That said, once you're open to looking elsewhere, a few additional storage opportunities open up. And SAS drives are perhaps the most attractive of these opportunities, allowing you to install enterprise-grade hardware for a fraction of the cost. All you need is to ensure compatibility with your PC.

6 things you must check when building a NAS with old PC parts

Some things to bear in mind when turning an old PC into a NAS.

5
By  Rich Edmonds

Buying used enterprise SAS drives might be the only deal left

Take advantage of the lower demand

Unlike consumer hard drives, NAS drives are optimized for 24/7 use and RAID error recovery. They aren't any faster in terms of read/write speeds, but feature a higher workload rating and vibration protection in multi-drive setups. SAS drives are designed for server use, so they naturally sport excellent reliability and massive capacity. They essentially marry the best of NAS and consumer drives, combining long-term reliability with affordable pricing.

The best thing is that once you start browsing SAS drives on eBay, you'll see they're even more affordable than regular HDDs. Since they cannot be used as-is with consumer PCs and require a Host Bus Adapter (HBA) card, they're tied to lower demand and, hence, lower prices. In terms of performance, they're rated for up to 12 Gb/s, which translates to 249 MB/s, which is faster than consumer and NAS drives.

The obvious roadblock here is the HBA card. Thankfully, you can source that on eBay, too, for as low as $30. Sellers don't always bundle the necessary cables with the card, so that will be an additional expense. You'll need a Mini-SAS cable that connects to the HBA card on one end and breaks out into SFF-8482 on the other end to connect to the SAS drive. Depending on the card, you can drive multiple 6 Gb/s or 12 Gb/s SAS drives simultaneously.

Before buying the card, ensure that it's flashed in Initiator Target (IT) mode (which most eBay listings are), so that the drives are exposed directly to the OS. Most NAS owners prefer LSI 9207-8i cards, but you can also get an LSI 9300-8i or LSI 9400-8i card for full 12 Gb/s support. These cards typically need x4 or x8 PCIe ports, so you'll need the respective spare slot on the motherboard.

Overall, your total investment for, say, three SAS drives, an HBA card, and the right cables can be as low as $500, which is quite impressive once you compare it with regular hard drive pricing.

An HBA SAS card costs $20 and turns any old PC into a storage server that rivals a prebuilt NAS

You'll have to hunt down ex-enterprise gear for that price, though

5
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Be ready to brave through a few quirks

It's still worth the hassle

It goes without saying that simply having the right adapter and cables won't eliminate the friction of using enterprise drives on your DIY NAS. Many SAS drives pulled from enterprise systems have a sector size of 520 or 528 bytes instead of the standard 512 bytes. For ZFS to work with your SAS drive, you'll need a reformat, which isn't a quick process on Linux at all.

Then, there's the hassle of making your HBA card work with your consumer motherboard. You may have to investigate the card's boot options, disable CSM in the BIOS, or remove the card's option ROM completely before it can allow the system to POST. Dell's LSI SAS2 cards are known not to work with some consumer motherboards unless you tape over the B5 and B6 pins on the card, isolating the card's SMBus from that of the motherboard.

Even if you manage to run the card properly, your SAS-powered NAS can be quite noisy, depending on the number of drives. These are server drives designed to operate in large racks, not compact consumer machines. Moreover, you'll need to cool both the card and the drives. Some sellers generously bundle a tiny fan with the HBA card, but most don't. You can use the same strategy with the drives by attaching a small fan directly facing them.

Lastly, power consumption can be a concern for some users, especially with 24/7 use. SAS drives need more power than SATA drives, so the power bills over the long term may be a factor in your purchase. The savings are considerable, so I'd recommend looking into used SAS drives seriously before you make the decision.

I built a NAS with enterprise SAS drives, and the hidden costs nearly matched new SATA drives

SAS is a standard that comes with its own unique pitfalls

By  Ty Sherback

Pre-owned enterprise drives are great for always-on systems

For your NAS or home server, buying used enterprise drives is better than expensive consumer or NAS hard drives. Even users who prefer SSDs should consider U.2 enterprise SSDs on the pre-owned market. You can save money while still enjoying great performance and superior reliability for your 24x7 machine.

item.title: 5 GPUs that are finally too old for modern games in 2026
item.itunes:title: 5 GPUs that are finally too old for modern games in 2026
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
GPU longevity is a touchy subject with gamers, since everyone has a different definition of what's "good enough." In a market where GPU pricing has gone off the rails, advocating an upgrade is not easy, but we sometimes have to admit the obvious. Every GPU reaches the end of the line sooner or later, no longer able to deliver a gaming experience that can be termed acceptable.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

My definition of "too old" is a graphics card that is incompatible with or can't consistently pump out 60+ FPS at 1080p in the latest AAA titles even with all the software trickery supporting it. Many gamers even consider 1080p a relic of the past, but we can't argue against the Steam Hardware & Software Survey. Based on this definition, the following five GPUs (or series of GPUs) have finally been left behind by modern gaming.

Throwing away your old GPU? — You might just be running out of VRAM

Your VRAM capacity can artificially limit your capable graphics card

1
By  Tanveer Singh

The GTX 1660 series was good while it lasted

It was a decent replacement for Pascal

I have a personal connection with Nvidia's GTX 1660 lineup, having used a GTX 1660 Ti for three years before cutting its lifecycle short by upgrading to an RTX 3080. For me, it was a significant upgrade over the GTX 1050 Ti, offering double the performance and even sustaining 1440p gaming for a while. The base GTX 1660 was a great budget card with 6GB of GDDR5 VRAM, with the GTX 1660 Super and 1660 Ti upgrading that to 6GB of GDDR6 memory.

Launched in 2019, the GTX 1660 Super/Ti was "going strong" till perhaps 2021–2022, delivering playable framerates at 1080p and even 1440p in some titles. However, once newer titles started mandating technologies like ray tracing and Resizable BAR (ReBAR), the GTX 1660 series had nothing to say. Granted, not every game justifies turning ray tracing on, but the GTX 1660 series fares poorly on performance, too.

You may argue that the GTX 1660 Super can still deliver 60+ FPS at 1080p in Cyberpunk 2077 or other years-old titles, but when considering the latest games, it's hard to argue in favor of the card. You can see it dip into the 40s even in slightly older titles like Alan Wake 2, Silent Hill f, or Dying Light: The Beast, even on optimized settings with FSR upscaling turned on at 1080p. So, it's time to leave the GTX 1660 series in the past.

I tested these "old" GPUs with 2026 AAA games, and the results were weirdly encouraging

Your old GPU might be more future-proof than you think

6
By  Samarveer Singh

The GTX 1070 series didn't age as well as some people think

The 8GB Pascal card stopped being powerful years ago

While Nvidia's GTX 1060 remained a fan-favorite GPU for several years after its launch, the GTX 1070 was poised to age far better than the 60-class card. The value for money of the GTX 1060 made it irresistible to the majority, but the GTX 1070 was significantly faster, had more VRAM, and was decidedly one of the higher-end SKUs of the Pascal lineup. And it did remain a powerful card for quite long, but after a decade, it doesn't rank any better than the GTX 1660 series.

You don't even need to look at the latest titles to see how the GTX 1070 isn't "going strong" anymore. Whether it's 2024's Ghost of Tsushima, 2023's Alan Wake 2, or even 2019's Red Dead Redemption 2, the GTX 1070 can't sustain 60+ FPS in these titles. Even in games where it delivers 60+ FPS on average, such as Cyberpunk 2077, you have to drop down to 1080p Medium settings.

The experience in games like Alan Wake 2, which demand mesh shaders, is terrible, since the Pascal series doesn't support the technology. Moreover, ray tracing and ReABR are absent as well, further limiting the GTX 1070's scope in 2026. Its 8GB VRAM isn't totally obsolete, but its PCIe 3.0 bus can tank your framerates if you run out of VRAM.

Is it just me or was the GTX 10 series the last great generation from Nvidia?

I feel like Nvidia peaked with the GTX 10 series GPUs, all things considered

7
By  Tanveer Singh

Even the GTX 1080 Ti has earned its rest

Let the old man go

The GTX 1080 Ti was naturally the last holdout of the Pascal lineup, allowing gamers to avoid an upgrade until just a few years ago. The fact that it rivals the RTX 3060 and RTX 2070 Super in rasterized performance just goes to show its longevity. And the 11GB VRAM easily allows the GTX 1080 Ti to punch above its weight. Alas, none of this can prevent the Pascal flagship from joining its siblings in the history books.

The same lack of mesh shader support and ray tracing that has aged several other GPUs on this list has stopped the GTX 1080 Ti in its tracks. When newer titles stop looking and performing like they're supposed to, you have to admit that your GPU has reached its end. While you may be able to enjoy some relatively modern games at 1080p at smooth framerates, the GTX 1080 Ti cannot be relied on for the latest titles in 2026.

It doesn't matter if you're running a newer title like Dying Light: The Beast or older ones like Ghost of Tsushima and Red Dead Redemption 2 — the GTX 1080 Ti isn't a consistent 1080p 60+ FPS card anymore.

The RTX 20 series has officially become Nvidia's Windows 7

The RTX 20 series became Nvidia's most stubborn survivor, just like Windows 7 became Microsoft's

13
By  Samarveer Singh

The RX 5700 series can't keep up

RDNA 1.0 is old news

Credit: Flickr

AMD deserves a spot on this list, even though we've seen them really rival Nvidia only recently. The RX 5700 and 5700 XT cards weren't bad at all; in fact, they were not much slower than the GTX 1080 Ti. The RX 5700 XT gave you 90% of the performance of the Pascal flagship. The RX 5700 series aged splendidly as owners refused to upgrade to expensive RX 6000 or RX 7000 models.

Seven years after launch, however, AMD's best RDNA 1 GPUs are far from what they used to be. Even at 1080p, you can't expect 60+ FPS in most of the latest titles. Games like The Last of Us Part 2 or Clair Obscur Expedition 33 can manage only around 50–55 FPS on average. With no mesh shaders or ray tracing hardware and disappointing FSR 3 support only, the RX 5700 and 5700 XT can safely be classified as "too old" in 2026.

I tested these "old" GPUs with 2026 AAA games, and the results were weirdly encouraging

Your old GPU might be more future-proof than you think

6
By  Samarveer Singh

The RTX 2060 series doesn't cut it in 2026

The cheapest RT cards aren't worth the branding

Credit: Source: ZMASLO via Wikimedia Commons

The Turing series is known for bringing real-time ray tracing to games in 2018, but it's also infamous for overpriced cards that offered little incentive for people to upgrade. item.itunes:title: I tried 3 Claude Code mods, and now waiting for it to finish is actually fun
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using Claude Code since its early days, and if there's one thing I've learned from my experience between now and then, it's that there's almost always a way to make it do more than you initially thought possible. Just when I think I've figured out everything the tool has to offer, Anthropic ends up launching yet another feature that changes the way I use it entirely.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Claude Code mods are the latest example of this. While there are already plenty of ways to customize Claude Code to your liking, mods take things a step further by letting you change how the tool itself looks and behaves. Naturally, I had to see just how much of a difference they could make. So, that's exactly what I did a few weeks ago, and it didn't take long for experimenting with different mods to turn into something I couldn't stop doing.

That's how I eventually stumbled upon three mods that have made my Claude Code sessions a whole lot more enjoyable.

cc-arcade

Claude does the work, I get to play

It's no fun waiting for Claude Code, or any AI agent for that matter, to complete a task. Sometimes, even the simplest tasks seem to take forever, and there's only so much you can do while waiting for the agent to finish working. As someone who gets distracted easily, I typically end up doing one of two things.

I either stare at the terminal window endlessly and wait for the spinner words to stop appearing. Or, what I like to describe as the worst of the two options, is I pick up my phone and go down a doomscrolling rabbit hole.

Neither is particularly productive, and the latter usually ends with me spending far more time on my phone than I originally intended. That's where cc-arcade comes in. Instead of staring at the terminal or reaching for my phone, I can play a game right inside Claude Code while it works on my task.

All this mod really does is add a collection of mini-games right above the Claude Code prompt, so you can keep yourself entertained while Claude works in the background. There are nine games to choose from, including classics like Snake, Tetris, Minesweeper, 2048, Flapp, Pong, Typing, Invaders, Pet, and even a simplified version of Doom.

I gave Claude Code control of my desktop for a week, and it automated things I didn't think were possible

I was seriously stunned.

59
By  Simon Batt

Once you've installed the mod, all you need to do is type /arcade into Claude Code, and you'll see a list of games to choose from. You can switch between them whenever you like, and the best part is that the game automatically pauses when Claude finishes its task, so you don't have to worry about missing a response.

There's also an auto mode that picks a game depending on what Claude is doing. For instance, if Claude has been working on something for over a minute, it'll suggest a longer game like Tetris or Snake. For shorter tasks, it'll pick something quicker, like Flappy or Pong.

My favorite little addition, though, is the virtual pet. It actually grows as Claude completes tasks, passes tests, edits files, and makes commits. It's completely unnecessary, of course, but that's precisely what makes it fun.

verbs

A little more personality never hurt anyone

Something I've always appreciated about Claude Code is the little personality Anthropic has given it. It's not something you'd typically expect from a terminal-based coding tool, but between the quirky spinner verbs that appear while it's working and the occasional witty message, Claude Code has always felt a little more playful than your average coding assistant.

In fact, I love its spinner verbs so much that I even wrote an entire article about how I added my own to the mix. Words like "Shenaniganing," "Flibbertigibbeting," and "Razzmatazzing" are entertaining enough on their own, but I figured there had to be a way to take things a step further.

That's where the verbs mod comes in. It's a mod that turns Claude Code's spinner verbs into little animated pixel-art illustrations that appear right above the loading indicator. There are animations for all 188 spinner verbs, so instead of just watching words like "Swirling," "Frolicking," or "Waddling" flash by, you get a tiny animation to go along with them.

It doesn't make Claude Code any faster, improve its responses, or add any particularly useful functionality. It's quite literally just a collection of animations that play while Claude works. But that's precisely what makes it so fun! Unlike some of the more elaborate mods, there's barely anything to configure. Once you've installed it and restarted Claude Code, the animations start appearing automatically.

mindful-claude

Inhale, exhale, let Claude do its thing

The last mod I've added to my Claude Code setup is something my therapist will likely appreciate. I'm terrible at taking breaks, especially when I'm caught up in work, and more often than not, I need an actual reminder to slow down and relax.

That's where Mindful Claude comes in. Instead of just watching the usual spinner words appear, you'll see a breathing animation right above the prompt that guides you through when to inhale, hold your breath, and exhale.

There are four breathing exercises to choose from, including box breathing, 4-7-8 breathing, coherent breathing, and physiological sighing. You can switch between them using the /breathe command, and even customize the animation's appearance with different styles like waves, ripples, and dots.

Of course, needing to remember to start a breathing exercise yourself would sort of defeat the entire purpose of this mod. This is why the animation automatically appears when Claude begins working on a task and disappears as soon as it finishes. You can even set a delay so it only appears when Claude has been working for a certain amount of time.

I set up Claude Code the way its creator does, and the difference is night and day

Who better to learn from than the person who made it?

19
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Though a few seconds of guided breathing aren't going to magically eliminate all your stress, I do appreciate the idea of turning those little pockets of waiting time into an opportunity to slow down, rather than immediately looking for something else to occupy my attention.

Now, none of these mods make any real difference to Claude Code's actual coding abilities. The code it spits out remains the same, and installing a bunch of mini-games or animated pixel art isn't suddenly going to make it a better coding assistant. However, that's not really the point.

If you're someone who spends hours working with Claude Code every day, you'd be surprised how much of a difference these little additions can make. Whether it's playing a quick game of Tetris while Claude work or simply being reminded to take a breather every now and then, they've all made my coding sessions a little more enjoyable.

cc-arcade

Claude does the work, I get to play

It's no fun waiting for Claude Code, or any AI agent for that matter, to complete a task. Sometimes, even the simplest tasks seem to take forever, and there's only so much you can do while waiting for the agent to finish working. As someone who gets distracted easily, I typically end up doing one of two things.

I either stare at the terminal window endlessly and wait for the spinner words to stop appearing. Or, what I like to describe as the worst of the two options, is I pick up my phone and go down a doomscrolling rabbit hole.

item.itunes:title: GPT-6.1 Terra brings more advanced computer agent use at a lower cost than Claude
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • GPT-6.1 Terra excels at multi-step computer tasks (Agent's Last Exam) and outperforms OpenAI models.
  • It's close to Claude Opus 5.5 performance but far cheaper—$1.01 vs $8.82.
  • Now available to Plus, Pro, Enterprise, Edu; 1M input tokens $1, 1M output tokens $5.

It seems a big pattern with GPT-6 is offering better performance for cheaper. Back when Anthropic revealed Claude Opus 5.5, OpenAI returned fire with GPT-6 Sol and Luna, which OpenAI claimed were both better yet more affordable than GPT-5.6. Now, OpenAI has pulled back the curtain and revealed GPT-6.1 Terra, which offers better computer use for less.

GPT-6.1 Terra is reportedly better than other OpenAI models at computer use

It scored pretty well in OpenAI's tests

Credit: OpenAI

On the OpenAI website, the company announced the release of GPT-6.1 Terra. OpenAI says it put 6.1 Terra through the paces with something called the "Agent's Last Exam," which is when an agent is tested to see if it can perform complex, multi-step computer tasks accurately.

You can see the results in the chart above. Each dot in a model's 'constellation' represents effort level, with the weakest on the left and the most powerful on the right. GPT-6.1 Terra on max effort—the dot on the far right of its line—overshadows all of OpenAI's models pretty effortlessly. It's also only 3.2 percentage points behind Claude Opus 5.5, while only costing $1.01 versus Claude's $8.82 bill.

Still, benchmarks are only a small window into how an LLM performs, and the real proof of adequacy will happen when people begin running it for their daily tasks. If you want to do that, GPT-6.1 Terra is now available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, and you can get 1 million input tokens for $1 and 1 million output tokens for $5.

I ditched $20 ChatGPT subscription and made Claude and Gemini work together for better results

What happens when you stop asking one AI to do everything and let two models collaborate?

item.title: The old Raspberry Pi 4 sitting in your drawer is worth more now than the day you bought it
item.itunes:title: The old Raspberry Pi 4 sitting in your drawer is worth more now than the day you bought it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every computing device, big or small, has seen an astounding price rise in the last few months. Memory and storage prices have quadrupled, and it's even hard to find “in-stock” products. Like everything else, the Raspberry Pi lineup is feeling the impact. Nothing is selling at its original price, and if you've got an older board like the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, it's a valuable commodity now.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The board comes in multiple memory versions, and each one now sells for double (or more) on e-commerce platforms. It's amusing that a board that's built on older technology has a higher cost. Usually, it's the other way round, but these are testing times. Let's discuss the current pricing of Raspberry Pi 4 Model B boards, and why it's still useful for home servers.

It's the worst time to buy an SBC

Difficult to digest pricing changes

The 1GB Raspberry Pi 4 Model B launched at $35 in 2019. The 2GB version costs $45, while you could snag a 4GB version for just $55. Even an 8GB version launched a year later at $75. Five years back, this seemed expensive. The Raspberry Pi 5 launched with just a $5 increase in price for the same memory capacity but a newer generation (LPDDR4X).

I lost interest in the older board because the memory was 1.5 times faster than the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, along with other upgrades. Currently, the 1GB Raspberry Pi 4 Model B version is the only one without a price hike. All the other versions have updated their pricing to reflect the memory apocalypse. The 2GB version retails for $67.50, while the more popular 4GB version is available for $83.

Raspberry Pi raises prices on several models with an unusual promise

Though, it's not all bad news

9
By  Rahul Naskar

These are official prices, but realistic pricing is $5–15 more for high-demand boards. I'm surprised by the 8GB version's price because it's more than double, and now sells for $165. The 1GB model prices have been kept intact because these boards find a lot of use in industrial applications. Higher-density memory (4GB and 8GB) has seen the biggest price spike, which is good news for hoarders and reseller markets.

Your old Raspberry Pi 4 is worth more

Enthusiasts can rejoice

The Raspberry Pi 4 lineup was modestly priced at its launch time. If you bought these boards anywhere between 2019 and early 2025, you would've escaped the inflated pricing. Some who have multiple Raspberry Pi 4 boards can make good money in the reseller or even box-sealed market. I don't expect average users to be sitting on piles of these SBC boxes. But small retailers and some hoarders will surely benefit from this unexpected opportunity.

If you've got a couple of spares and have upgraded to Raspberry Pi 5s, you can earn some profit in the used market. However, it's not a great time for consumers. They have to pay more money for an older-generation board, and the limited availability makes it even worse. Even the used boards will sell for a few dollars less than the current price. So, it'll be a bad couple of years for anyone looking to build a cheap mini server.

5 of the best budget-friendly SBCs

Not all SBCs cost an arm and a leg

1
By  Ayush Pande

A refurbished thin client seems like a better proposition now. I recently bought one for about $45 with 8GB of memory and a 128GB SSD, and both components are new. So the price-to-performance ratio doesn't seem appealing enough. I also purchased a 1GB Raspberry Pi 4 Model B for $35, and adding an SD card bumped its price to $60. Apart from the low power usage, there is nothing in favor of either the Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 lineups. But that doesn't make your old Raspberry Pi 4 Model B a bad device.

Putting the SBC to good use

Endless possibilities

Ignoring the current prices, the Raspberry Pi has the best software support and community, and that advantage is hard to beat. I've tried boards from other brands, but they are nowhere close to this one. The new Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, except for the 1GB version, is not a smart pick. But if you already own the board and haven't built anything with it in a while, now’s the chance.

Even the lowest memory capacity in the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B lineup can act as a great local cloud storage alternative, a DNS sinkhole and server, or a password manager. I've run some of these projects on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, so the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B will undoubtedly have better performance. The 1GB memory versions can run most of the self-hosted tools without falling short of memory.

The Raspberry Pi 5 has become so expensive that my cheap DDR3 SBCs make more sense for most projects

Old DDR3 single-board computers actually beat the Raspberry Pi on price

4
By  Ayush Pande

The focus has also shifted to more lightweight tools like BentoPDF, Papra, Vaultwarden, and the board can run multiple tools like these. Another advantage is that it's a full-sized board with all the necessary ports. The Ethernet port and additional USB ports are an advantage for network-focused projects like Pi-Hole.

Even the dedicated 3.5 mm audio port is great for audio-focused projects like reviving old speakers that lack HDMI. If you use a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W or even the Raspberry Pi 5, you'll have to buy an additional USB DAC to get the job done. While it may not support native NVMe SSDs or AI HAT modules, it can still offer better storage speeds via the USB 3.0 connection ports.

Surprising value increase

Old hardware tends to depreciate, but this memory and storage apocalypse has turned the tables for them. An old SBC like the Raspberry Pi 4 was slowly becoming less popular after the launch of the Raspberry Pi 5. But the current pricing suggests otherwise, and even with a huge spike from the original rates, the demand is there. The 4GB and 8GB editions seem to be out of stock everywhere because anyone looking for serious computing projects will want them. Meanwhile, you can rejoice a bit because your old board is worth more now.

item.title: Your TV's HDMI ports aren't equal, and manufacturers aren't telling you the whole story

item.itunes:summary:
It's an age-old problem, and one that's a little too common for comfort — someone you know spends $500, $1000, or even $2000 on a brand-new TV and a console, but the TV refuses to deliver the features listed on the product page.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The showroom floor salesperson never stopped talking about 4K resolution, 120Hz refresh rates, variable refresh rate, and even HDMI 2.1 support, but at home, none of those features seem to work. From the outside, nothing appears immediately or obviously broken. Even your streaming apps will work perfectly, your console will behave normally, and you might even think you're getting the specs the TV promised.

And yet, there's a pretty good chance that the problem isn't your console, HDMI cable, or even the TV's own processing. It's something far less obvious, and sadly, far more common, which is something manufacturers do a rather terrible job at explaining.

Your TV's HDMI ports aren't created equal

The four ports have four very different capabilities

My friend discovered this the hard way after buying a PlayStation 5 Pro earlier last month. Their decision to buy a $700 at a scalper-raised price of $1100 notwithstanding, the console went pretty nicely with their LG C5 OLED TV they bought earlier this year. The problem, of course, was that YouTube and Netflix on the console happily displayed 4K content, but launching a game immediately dropped the console's output to 1080p.

Nothing was really broken, though. That was because the console was connected to the TV's third HDMI port, which could deliver 4K but not at 120Hz (the console's default refresh rate). This was because the first port, the HDMI eARC port, was connected to the soundbar, and the second port went towards an Apple TV 4K.

This is the kind of problem that makes people question their own perfectly good hardware. The PS5 Pro supports the features, and the TV advertises them, but a seemingly insignificant connection determines whether those expensive components can deliver the experience you paid for.

Stop shopping for HDMI 2.1 cables, because they don't actually exist

The product stickers on your HDMI cable are lying to you

2
By  Samarveer Singh

You'd imagine that every manufacturer labels their capable ports with a 4K120 marking, but that's not the case, either. Plenty of TVs leave you scratching your head when you read the manual. Certain televisions even have HDMI 2.1 ports with different bandwidth limits, meaning the version number alone tells you surprisingly little about what each connection can handle.

And then there's the television that technically supports everything you want, just not through the port you've plugged into. Buying a premium television and unlocking a budget-model experience is not something I'd wish for anyone.

I let Claude Code debloat my Smart TV, and it exposed a bigger problem

Software is only part of the problem

5
By  Anurag Singh

Why your TV can't do everything through every port

Bandwidth is expensive, and eARC complicates everything

The real problem is that most TVs have several HDMI ports, but only the first two are truly capable, while the rest share bandwidth and capabilities. On the surface, it's pretty much a cost-cutting method manufacturers use. However, streaming apps like YouTube or Netflix rarely expose this problem, since most video content only runs at 24fps, 30fps, or 60fps. As such, 4K60fps content runs pretty smoothly even in the "wrong" port.

Only when you launch a game configured for 4K at 120Hz will a port lacking sufficient bandwidth show itself and force the console to lower its resolution to maintain that high refresh rate, since the connection just can't carry everything simultaneously.

The economics are simple to understand, infuriating as they may be.

Full-bandwidth HDMI 2.1 implementations require capable chipsets and supporting hardware. As such, manufacturers tend to reserve their best connections for a subset of ports instead of equipping all four HDMI ports on a TV with equal capabilities.

The bigger problem, however, from a user standpoint, is eARC (enhanced Audio Return Channel). It sends high-quality audio from your TV to a soundbar or receiver, and audiophiles can't live without it (nor should they have to). On some TVs, though, the port that offers the best gaming capabilities (4K120) is also the only one designated for eARC, making it the only port you can connect to your soundbar, and thus forcing you to choose between uncompromised gaming and convenient audio connectivity.

Sure, you can route audio through other connections (sometimes), but that means getting extra cables, configuration headaches, or even compromised functionality if the TV or its software doesn't support the workaround.

I don't use HDMI, and I never will

Miss me with the inferior connection for my PC.

19
By  Joe Rice-Jones

This is a manufactured usability problem

Stop making customers decode the specifications

I genuinely don't think this is a customer knowledge problem at all, though. If you buy a $1,000 TV, you shouldn't have to do detective work to figure out which of its four ports delivers the advertised experience and which device in my setup goes with which port.

And yet, manufacturers routinely hide these distinctions in specification sheets with tiny labels and manuals nobody reads until something goes wrong. Even worse, if your TV is mounted against a wall, those labels become practically useless — a design failure that is all too avoidable, sadly.

This isn't a problem limited to console gamers, either. If you're a PC gamer, you could also find yourself unable to achieve 4K at 144Hz. Even home-theater enthusiasts can lose their beloved Dolby Vision compatibility through an inadequately equipped port. Mac mini owners, too, can discover that their display's supposedly capable connection has limitations that nobody warned them about.

The problem is that manufacturers know these distinctions matter, but they also know that printing "HDMI 2.1" across a product page is better than "our best features are only in two of the four HDMI ports." The power-user percentage worldwide will always remain a sliver compared to the millions of people who can buy expensive TVs without specialist knowledge. If a TV can't deliver its headline specifications through every port, it should disclose that limitation prominently before checkout.

Why I stopped buying smart TVs, and what I bought instead

Remember when smart features worked for us, instead of against us?

15
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Manufacturers aren't going to become completely honest any time soon

The next time you're shopping for a television, don't stop at the refresh rate, panel technology, or whatever impressive acronym the marketing department has decided to plaster across the box. Look at the number of HDMI ports that can actually deliver the full experience you expect from your devices, because that is the specification that deserves the most attention, depending on how many things you plan to plug into the TV.

A new TV should simplify a user's entertainment setup, but far too often, it ends up costing people an entire weekend of troubleshooting as they try to connect a console, soundbar, and streaming box. Manufacturers can do better, and reviewers should be far more aggressive about calling out these limitations before recommending a television to millions of buyers.

However, that's far too optimistic. Until that changes, treat the HDMI port count as a primary buying criterion instead of an afterthought. After all, there's little point paying for features that your television makes unnecessarily difficult to use.
